name: Pediatric anterolateral approach to the humeral shaft
corridor: Anterolateral interval between biceps/brachialis medially and the mobile wad laterally, splitting brachialis in the plane between the radial and musculocutaneous nerves to reach the anterior humerus

positioning.text: Position supine with the arm on a hand table and the shoulder to distal arm accessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the deltopectoral interval proximally and the biceps and mobile wad interval distally.

incision.text: Follow a line from the interval between biceps and the mobile wad distally to the deltopectoral interval proximally.

superficial_interval.text: Incise the fascia between biceps/brachialis and the mobile wad, retract the biceps medially and the mobile wad laterally, identifying the cephalic vein proximally.

deep_interval.text: Split the brachialis in the plane between the radial and musculocutaneous nerves to keep its dual innervation and protect the radial nerve where it perforates the lateral intermuscular septum.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, the biceps/brachialis and mobile wad interval, the split brachialis, and the anterior humerus.

structures_at_risk.text: The radial nerve perforating the lateral intermuscular septum, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm distally, and the musculocutaneous nerve are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The distal lateral humerus where the radial nerve perforates the septum is the danger zone.

retraction_hazards.text: Split brachialis in its midline to protect the radial nerve laterally and keep the mobile wad retraction gentle.

exposure.text: Exposes the anterior surface of the proximal and mid humerus.

limitations.text: Distal extension is limited by the radial nerve, and very distal fractures may need a separate exposure.

indications.text: Indicated for plating of pediatric proximal and midshaft humeral fractures.

closure.text: Close the subcutaneous tissues and skin in layers with absorbable sutures.

complications.text: Complications include radial nerve palsy, lateral forearm cutaneous nerve injury, and wound problems.

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric proximal or midshaft humeral fracture is plated through an anterior interval

questions.question: In what nerve plane is the brachialis split in the anterolateral humeral approach?
questions.answer: Between the radial and musculocutaneous nerves.

questions.question: Where does the radial nerve enter the anterior compartment?
questions.answer: By perforating the lateral intermuscular septum distally.

questions.question: Why split brachialis rather than take it off one side?
questions.answer: To preserve its dual radial and musculocutaneous innervation.
